findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_retry_path.mjs (new) - EVERY /rest/v1/ read failed with a 500, then the network released and the retry pressed. ★THE INDUCTION IS TOTAL, NOT PARTIAL, AND THAT CHANGED THE ANSWER. The availability lens fails a SUBSET of reads and reported 'affordances: 0' for pages that demonstrably DO render a Retry on other paths. Failing every request is what actually reaches a page's error branch. ★AND BOTH CLAUSES ARE MEASURED, because the second is the one that ships broken: a retry must RE-ATTEMPT and the failure must CLEAR. hive proved why - its first fix sent 3 fresh reads and left the page byte-for-byte unchanged, because it re-rendered from a cache still holding the failed state. A retry that re-attempts and does not recover is worse than none: it invites pressing again. ★THE ROSTER, so no page's verdict rests on its own reading alone: PASS 6 (hive, logbook, inventory, skillmatrix, public-feed, resume) | NO-RETRY 9 | NO-RECOVER 3 | NO-ATTEMPT 1 | SILENT 3. ★THE COMPONENT ALREADY EXISTS - THIS IS ADOPTION, NOT DESIGN. whListError(el, message, onRetry) in utils.js renders the inline error WITH a working Retry, and 16 pages already import it. Six pages passing is what separates 'nobody built this' from 'not every read path routes through it'. FOR THIS PAGE: it SAYS a failure happened and offers NOTHING TO PRESS. Telling someone to check their connection is advice; a control they can press is a path, and the oracle asks for the second. The fix is to route this read's error branch through whListError, which this roster already uses on six pages - a per-path edit, not a design decision.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.
evidence.value_checked: 400-insert burst -> 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' HINT logbook_daily_user; hive tier raises 54000 'cumulative quota exceeded' + archive hint; 0 probe rows survived rollback

findings.title: FAILS THE FIRST CLAUSE ONLY, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 3 reads answered 500: this page
findings.detail: FAILS THE FIRST CLAUSE ONLY, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 3 reads answered 500: this page DOES say the primary is down, in domain language - **'Could not load PM compliance - Overdue PMs are unknown right now, not zero. Reload before treating this plant as compliant.'** - and it dashes its tiles rather than zeroing them (`stat-overdue`, `stat-duesoon` and `stat-ontrack` all read a dash). So it does not pretend nothing happened, and that half is genuinely done. WHAT IS MISSING IS THE FALLBACK ITSELF, and no page-level fix can supply it: THERE IS NO READ FALLBACK ON THIS PLATFORM, AND THAT IS PROVEN FROM THE SERVICE WORKER'S SOURCE RATHER THAN INFERRED. `sw.js` handles API traffic in one branch - `if (url.includes('supabase.co') || url.includes('fonts.goog') ...) e.respondWith(fetch(e.request).catch(() => new Response('', { status: 503 })))` (sw.js:195-200) - so a failed read resolves to an EMPTY 503 body. And `cache.put` appears **nowhere in the file**, so no API response is ever stored: `caches.match()` cannot hit for a `/rest/v1/` URL because nothing put one there. The 26-entry `SHELL_FILES` precache holds HTML, CSS and JS only. SO THE FIRST CLAUSE CANNOT BE SATISFIED FOR READS BY CONSTRUCTION - there is nothing to engage. The offline layer this platform does have is for WRITES (the `wh_logbook_offline` / `wh_dayplanner_offline` / `wh_assethub_offline` IndexedDB queues), which is a different oracle. That makes the second clause the whole test: does the surface say the primary is down, or does it pretend nothing happened? SO THIS ROW IS NOT A PAGE DEFECT BUT A PLATFORM GAP, recorded here because the oracle asks for a fallback and there is none to engage. It is banked as a finding rather than a pass so the debt stays visible, and rather than `declared-na` because the subject is real - the platform HAS an offline layer, it just serves writes only. NOTE: the asset list still reads 'No assets yet - Tap the + button to add your first asset' under the same failure, which is recorded on this page's fail_500 row. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: cache the last successful read per surface (an IndexedDB mirror beside the existing write queues, or a `cache.put` on the API branch keyed by query) and label the rendered copy with its age - 'showing your last synced copy from 14:20'. That is one central mechanism, not 22 page fixes, which is the CENTRALIZE-FIRST call. MEASURED TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS, so the reading does not rest on one injection style. (1) Every `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request answered with a synthetic 500 at `window.fetch`, `/auth/v1/` left alone so the session survives, interceptions counted and a zero-interception run refused as vacuous. (2) A genuine `setOffline(true)` navigation with the service-worker cache WARM. THE SECOND METHOD TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS TO GET HONEST, WHICH IS WHY IT IS TRUSTWORTHY NOW. Navigating to `/workhive/logbook.html` offline served the branded offline shell every time - not because the page is unavailable offline, but because `SHELL_FILES` precaches ROOT paths (`/logbook.html`) and the `/workhive/` prefix is a different cache key. Measured at the path the cache actually holds, the real page is served. A verdict from the prefixed path would have described a cache miss and called it product behaviour. AND ONE LIMIT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: under Playwright's `setOffline(true)`, `navigator.onLine` still read **true** and `wh-conn-chip` still read 'Online' (hidden). The app's own offline DETECTION therefore never fired, so this reading covers 'the primary is down' but NOT 'the app knows it is offline'. The absence of an offline banner is consequently NOT charged against the page here. A probe that wants that claim must also override `navigator.onLine` and dispatch the `offline` event.

findings.detail: RECORDED OWED WITH A MIXED IN-FLIGHT READING - not passed, not failed, because the evidence genuinely points both ways and one more measurement decides it. With reads held in flight this page shows explicit loading vocabulary AND 3 dash sentinels (so part of the surface sentinels correctly), while 3 bare numbers are on screen, 3 of them zeros. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER THOSE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS OR STATIC HTML DEFAULTS. The KPI heroes ship as `0` in the markup and are overwritten when data lands, so a zero seen mid-load may be untouched initial markup rather than a computed claim - and from outside the two are indistinguishable. dayplanner in this same pass showed 3 in-flight zeros against 2 settled zeros, i.e. its zeros were mostly REAL values, which is exactly why a count alone cannot decide. TO FINISH - one targeted probe, no guesswork: snapshot each KPI element's textContent before the reads resolve and again after, and compare against that element's value in the static HTML. A zero that never changes and equals the markup default is a placeholder; a zero written by the render is a fabricated answer. MEASURED BY DELAYING THE PAGE'S OWN READS, NOT BY GUESSING AT A SLOW NETWORK. Every /rest/v1/ and /rpc/ request is wrapped in a 6-second delay before being forwarded to the real fetch (auth left untouched so the identity guard still works), and the surface is read at 2.2s - i.e. WHILE the reads are provably still in flight. Interceptions are COUNTED and a verdict over zero is refused as vacuous. THE ORACLE IS WHETHER A SLOW READ IS SHOWN AS SLOW rather than answered with a fabricated value, so the in-flight state IS the measurement. Three positive signals are collected independently - skeleton/shimmer/aria-busy elements, explicit loading vocabulary in the body, and dash sentinels - alongside the two things that would betray it: how many bare numbers are on screen, and whether any false-empty sentence has appeared. AN HONEST INSTRUMENT LIMIT, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the post-delay sample taken 7s later was still MID-LOAD on three pages (skeletons still present), because 6s per read across sequential reads exceeds that wait. So the settled comparison is NOT used for any verdict here - only the in-flight reading. Using a still-loading sample as the 'after' picture would have made every page look permanently broken.

findings.title: CLASSIFIED WITH EVIDENCE rather than left un-attempted.
findings.detail: CLASSIFIED WITH EVIDENCE rather than left un-attempted. This oracle asks that offline the write be REFUSED before firing and the person told nothing was sent - so before it can be graded, this view's committing write has to be identified and its CLASS settled, because the platform deliberately splits them: field capture QUEUES, while approvals, locked, financial, moderation and role writes are online-only-with-clarity (the generic drain carries no optimistic lock and those writes depend on one). Grading a queue-backed write against a refusal is wrong in both directions - green credits a refusal that must not exist, red calls a working feature a defect. The test is per-FUNCTION, not per-page: inventory, community and skillmatrix each show BOTH classes on one page. See PAGE_TESTBANK_ROADMAP.md SS6 for the sibling offline_queued cell proposed for the queue side, and tools/prove_offline_queued.mjs which grades it. THIS VIEW IS QUEUE-CLASS. Its write is registered with the page's own offline queue (window._whPmQueue over wh_pm_offline, table pm_completions), so offline it is HELD and the person is told it will sync - which is the correct behaviour and the opposite of what this oracle asks for. Refusing it would remove offline capture from someone working with no signal, which is the mistake I made on community's submitPost this session and had to revert after it removed working offline posting. WHAT THIS ROW NEEDS INSTEAD: the offline_queued oracle - zero server writes, POSITIVE acceptance evidence (the queue store grew), the will-sync message, no false refusal wording, and on reconnect a drain that happens EXACTLY ONCE. THIS IS THE ONE I WAS ONE EDIT FROM BREAKING. submitCompletion looked like an obvious guard target - a PM completion is a compliance record - and guarding it would have removed offline PM completion from a technician in a plant basement. Its queue entry even carries a true idempotency key (pm_completions_dedup_uidx on scope_item_id + worker_name + date), so a retry after a lost response cannot double-count. The page's OTHER writes - toggleAutoHail, saveEditPMAsset, saveAsset, saveNewTask on pm_scope_items / pm_assets - are configuration and asset records, not capture, and were guarded.

findings.title: MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean.
findings.detail:
MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. RETRY PATH - FAILS, and the half that is certain is the half that matters. Under an injected 500 this page offers ZERO retry affordances: no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'refresh' control. That is confirmed TWO independent ways - the lens counted affordances:0, and a separate direct probe that 500'd every /rest/v1/ request and scanned the whole document for a retry control also found none. A person whose data failed to load has nothing to press. ★ONE HALF OF THIS VERDICT IS INSTRUMENT-DEPENDENT AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN BANKED AS FACT: the lens also reported saysFailure:True. My direct probe, which failed EVERY read rather than the subset the lens induces, and which scanned the whole page rather than <main>, found that this page DOES say something failed under a total outage. So the page's failure MESSAGING may be better than the lens's number suggests - a partial induction can leave a surface half-populated and quiet. The missing retry CONTROL is not in doubt; the missing failure SENTENCE is, on this page. WHY IT IS NOT BANKED GREEN ANYWAY: the oracle asks for a retry PATH, and a failure a person cannot act on is the shape this family exists to catch - 'a failure that offers a retry which does not re-attempt is worse than one that offers none', and offering none at all is the floor of that same scale.

★RETRACTED CONTEXT ON THIS ROW'S RECORDED TALLY: it lists rate_limit_legible as 1P/21F. That figure is true of THIS LENS and misleading about the platform, and is retracted as evidence of any gap. 42 rate_limit_legible rows are banked green on a 2026-08-09 induction against the REAL limit - 400 logbook inserts inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK as an authenticated member, refused with 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. THE VERDICT ON THIS ROW'S OWN KEY IS UNAFFECTED - it rests on its own induction, which landed (inductionLanded > 0).

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_retry_path.mjs (new) - EVERY /rest/v1/ read failed with a 500, then the network released and the retry pressed.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_retry_path.mjs (new) - EVERY /rest/v1/ read failed with a 500, then the network released and the retry pressed. ★THE INDUCTION IS TOTAL, NOT PARTIAL, AND THAT CHANGED THE ANSWER. The availability lens fails a SUBSET of reads and reported 'affordances: 0' for pages that demonstrably DO render a Retry on other paths. Failing every request is what actually reaches a page's error branch. ★AND BOTH CLAUSES ARE MEASURED, because the second is the one that ships broken: a retry must RE-ATTEMPT and the failure must CLEAR. hive proved why - its first fix sent 3 fresh reads and left the page byte-for-byte unchanged, because it re-rendered from a cache still holding the failed state. A retry that re-attempts and does not recover is worse than none: it invites pressing again. ★THE ROSTER, so no page's verdict rests on its own reading alone: PASS 6 (hive, logbook, inventory, skillmatrix, public-feed, resume) | NO-RETRY 9 | NO-RECOVER 3 | NO-ATTEMPT 1 | SILENT 3. ★THE COMPONENT ALREADY EXISTS - THIS IS ADOPTION, NOT DESIGN. whListError(el, message, onRetry) in utils.js renders the inline error WITH a working Retry, and 16 pages already import it. Six pages passing is what separates 'nobody built this' from 'not every read path routes through it'. FOR THIS PAGE: it SAYS a failure happened and offers NOTHING TO PRESS. Telling someone to check their connection is advice; a control they can press is a path, and the oracle asks for the second. The fix is to route this read's error branch through whListError, which this roster already uses on six pages - a per-path edit, not a design decision.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: this view fires no read of its own, so the oracle has no denominator here - recorded as vacuous rather than counted as proof
evidence.checked: WHY THIS ROW WAS RE-MEASURED. Its previous evidence was IDENTICAL to the V1 row's on the same page - a KPI-tile reading taken at page load - because the banking loop selected rows by oracle name and swept both views with one page-level measurement. Fourteen V2 rows across the platform carried a measurement of a view they never visited, which is R7's exact failure: a claim resting on something other than what it names. The count did not move; the evidence did. DECLARED-NA ON A MEASURED DENOMINATOR (rail R10), proven live rather than inferred from the source. Reaching this view takes two hops - `openDetail(<assetId>)` on an asset row, then `markDone(<scopeItemId>)` on a scope item - and with the delay armed at the second hop the sheet opened visible having fired **0 reads**. Its contents came entirely from state already in memory: 'Task Completed / General visual + cleanliness / Cleaver-Brooks CB-700-200 / Completed: Aug 10, 2026'. THE SOURCE AGREES, WHICH IS WHY THE ZERO IS TRUSTWORTHY RATHER THAN A MISSED REQUEST: markDone() at pm-scheduler.html:1997 does `scopeItems.find(i => i.id === scopeItemId)` and returns early if the item is absent, so the sheet CANNOT open before its data exists. A view that cannot render ahead of its data has no slow-read state to be honest or dishonest about. Emptiness recorded, not counted. MEASURED WITH THE DELAY ARMED AFTER INITIAL LOAD, which is what makes a V2 view measurable at all. A modal or thread cannot be opened while the feed that renders its opener is still pending, so the fetch wrapper starts INERT and is armed only once the page has settled; the view is then opened and its OWN read is the one held in flight. Every reading below is refused unless `resolved === 0` at measurement time and at least one request was intercepted, so neither a vacuous run nor an already-resolved one can be reported as a pass.

scenarios.question: IDENTITY - authN from the JWT, authZ at the server, boundaries stated as boundaries and never rendered as emptiness
scenarios.oracle: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: worker (role floor on scheduling) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 8 of its 9 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); logbook (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 11 read relation(s), 9 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, hive_audit_log, hive_members, logbook, pm_assets, pm_completions, pm_scope_items, project_links, projects).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

scenarios.oracle: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: two_context (double completion race) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

So a true GATEWAY fact was reported as 22 page defects it does not imply. evidence.asserts: the on-time basis is stated as each PM's OWN interval, which is what it actually is - no hidden grace window, and the rolling nature of the period named too
evidence.checked: The surface renders '72.1% done on time (last 90 days, within each PM's own interval) - 114 of 408 ran late', and every part of that label was traced to the function it describes. THE TOLERANCE: get_pm_ontime_delivery counts a completion on time when 'completed_at <= prev_at + (frequency_days || ' days')::interval' - so there is NO separate grace period; the tolerance IS the PM's own frequency, meaning a monthly PM done on day 30 is on time, the same PM on day 35 is late, and a quarterly PM has ninety days of room. Saying 'within each PM's own interval' rather than 'on time' is therefore load-bearing, because the phrase 'on time' reads like a fixed grace window and it is not. THE WINDOW: rendered as 'LAST 90 days' rather than '90 days' because the period is ROLLING - 'now() - (p_period_days || ' days')::interval' - which matters for anyone comparing this month's figure to last month's. And the page's own comment records why the window must be labelled at all: the only other window on screen is the 'DUE SOON (14D)' tile one card away, so an unlabelled 90-day figure sitting beside a labelled 14-day one is worse than merely unhelpful. THE SECOND NUMBER: SMRP 2.1.1 credits a PM completed anywhere inside its period, so a program can read well while a quarter of the work ran past its own frequency - which is why the stricter on-time figure is printed BESIDE the flattering compliance one, with the late COUNT ('114 of 408 ran late') in the form a supervisor can act on.
evidence.value_checked: page: '79% PM compliance (SMRP, last 90 days) · 72.1% done on time (last 90 days, within each PM's own interval) · 114 of 408 ran late'. get_pm_ontime_delivery: on time iff completed_at <= prev_at + (frequency_days||' days')::interval (no separate grace). Window: now() - (p_period_days||' days')::interval = rolling.

findings.title: false-green-withdrawn 2026-08-06, found by self-audit: banked on 'skeleton observed (div.wh-cardskel, aria-busy=true, t=138-335ms) + CLS 0.0144/0/0', which does not establish the oracle's claim that the skeleton RESERVES space. Re-measured with a VISIBILITY filter across 2 cold loads: visFrames 0 while anyFrames was 37 and 9 - the element exists in the DOM for dozens of frames and paints in none, so it reserves nothing and CLS is 0 by a different mechanism. Identical to report-sender-127, withdrawn the same day. The root error was mine: an UNFILTERED [aria-busy=true] query proves a busy state is DECLARED, not that a loading state is PAINTED, and I let the word 'observed' carry both. TO CLOSE: either render the card skeleton visibly (then re-measure visFrames > 0 AND CLS <= 0.1 over 3 loads), or bank declared-na with 'no visible loading state on this surface' as the reason.

findings.title: MEASURED INSIDE THIS VIEW, with tools/prove_view_contrast.mjs - 34 of 37 drivable registry views carried text to measure, ZERO failing.
findings.detail: MEASURED INSIDE THIS VIEW, with tools/prove_view_contrast.mjs - 34 of 37 drivable registry views carried text to measure, ZERO failing. ★WHY A VIEW-SCOPED PROVER HAD TO BE BUILT FOR THIS: a page-level sweep of all 22 pages (tools/prove_page_contrast.mjs) found the platform clean and settled NOTHING here, because every owed contrast row in these banks is authored against V2 or V3 - the dialogs - while their V1 siblings were already green. Banking a page-default reading onto a V2 row is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error that has already put 14 rows in this bank carrying another view's verdict. The view is opened through tools/dialog_targets.mjs, the same shared registry ten other provers use, so the view graded here is the view they grade. WCAG 2.x is measured with the composited probe: the background is blended UP the ancestor chain, because a translucent tint over a dark card is not the colour the stylesheet names, and text over a gradient is recorded as UNMEASURABLE rather than being compared against a canvas it never sits on - the shape that once reported ratio exactly 1.00 for perfectly legible text. NOT BANKED: this view yielded ZERO measurable samples (10 unmeasurable), so there is no denominator and a pass would be vacuous. The cause is structural rather than a probe fault, and it was verified by tracing the paint chain: the dialog's inner card is a TRANSLUCENT GRADIENT - linear-gradient(145deg, rgba(42,61,88,0.6) ...) - over a rgba(0,0,0,0.75) scrim over the page. WCAG 2.x is a ratio between TWO colours, and there is no single background colour here to be the second one. THE APCA SIBLING OF THIS ROW IS NOT AFFECTED and was measured normally, because that lens averages the gradient's stops instead of demanding one flat colour - which is why the platform treats APCA as the primary contrast oracle on this dark shell. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: sample the RENDERED PIXELS around each glyph from a screenshot of this view, which is the only way to obtain the real second colour behind text that sits on a gradient. That is a buildable instrument, not a ceiling - it is simply not built yet, and this row stays owed until it is.

observed.blocker: translucent gradient card over a translucent scrim - no single bg colour exists

WCAG 2.x is measured with the composited probe: the background is blended UP the ancestor chain, because a translucent tint over a dark card is not the colour the stylesheet names, and text over a gradient is recorded as UNMEASURABLE rather than being compared against a canvas it never sits on - the shape that once reported ratio exactly 1.00 for perfectly legible text. NOT BANKED: this view yielded ZERO measurable samples (8 unmeasurable), so there is no denominator and a pass would be vacuous. The cause is structural rather than a probe fault, and it was verified by tracing the paint chain: the dialog's inner card is a TRANSLUCENT GRADIENT - linear-gradient(145deg, rgba(42,61,88,0.6) ...) - over a rgba(0,0,0,0.75) scrim over the page. WCAG 2.x is a ratio between TWO colours, and there is no single background colour here to be the second one. THE APCA SIBLING OF THIS ROW IS NOT AFFECTED and was measured normally, because that lens averages the gradient's stops instead of demanding one flat colour - which is why the platform treats APCA as the primary contrast oracle on this dark shell. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: sample the RENDERED PIXELS around each glyph from a screenshot of this view, which is the only way to obtain the real second colour behind text that sits on a gradient. That is a buildable instrument, not a ceiling - it is simply not built yet, and this row stays owed until it is.

findings.title: FAILS: with 9 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 2364 characters before the refusal and 882 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than ID
findings.detail: FAILS: with 9 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 2364 characters before the refusal and 882 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than IDENTITY, because this platform has already shipped that exact inversion - a 42501 rendered as 'your session has expired', which sends a signed-IN person to re-authenticate for a problem authentication cannot fix, and 401/403 collapsed into one message so neither audience got a true statement. ZERO of the 16 graded pages made that mistake on this run. utils.js:1607 whIsAuthFailure() is why: it returns FALSE for status 403 with the comment 'authenticated, and refused. Not a session problem', and documents 42501 as insufficient_privilege. That discrimination is holding. HOW THE REFUSAL WAS INDUCED, and why it is the real branch: every Supabase REST read is answered with the body PostgREST actually sends for a row-level-security refusal - HTTP 403 with {"code":"42501","message":"permission denied for table"} - so the page's own error handling takes the same path it would in production. The patch is on window.fetch, NOT page.route, because a warm service worker serves from cache and bypasses route interception; it is installed with addInitScript in a context closed after each page so it cannot leak. NON-WRITING: it makes a READ return 403. THE INJECTION PROVES ITSELF: every intercepted call increments a counter, and a page where the counter is zero is UNGRADED rather than judged. That guard exists because the first version of this prover silently did nothing - a regex written inside a template literal collapsed to one that terminates at its second character, so the init script was a SyntaxError, every read succeeded normally, and the prover reported 'the reads were all refused and the page said nothing' while nothing had been refused at all. Hit counts on this run ranged from 8 to 42 per page. AND THE SIGNAL MUST APPEAR: the same page is read WITHOUT the injection first, and if its ordinary copy already matches the refusal vocabulary the page is UNGRADED - which is exactly what happened to skillmatrix, whose normal text contains a matching phrase. Without that control a page whose everyday copy happens to say 'cannot' would pass for free. THE SYNTHESIS - THIS IS ONE MISSING SURFACE, NOT 15 PAGE BUGS. Of 16 graded pages: 13 said NOTHING AT ALL when every read was refused, 2 showed only a GENERIC error ('Analysis failed, check console'; 'Achievements failed to load.'), and 1 passed. The platform already has the pieces - a central WRITE-failure message and the correct 401-vs-403 discriminator in utils.js - but there is no equivalent on the READ path, so a refused read renders as dashes or blanks with no explanation. On logbook the numbers '516 entries 30 machines 6 open' became '- entries - machines - open' with the body text identical to the character (1107 before and after) and not one word about why. A person cannot tell 'there is no data' from 'the load failed' from 'you are not allowed', and those three call for three different actions. THE FIX IS ONE ADOPTION, not 15 edits: give the read path the same treatment the write path already has. This independently reproduces a finding already recorded as 'the message already exists; the gap is ADOPTION on the read path'. SCOPE: V1, the page as it loads, and READ refusal only - a refused WRITE is a different path with its own central message, and is not claimed here. 5 of the 22 pages are excluded from the sweep because they are public or have no authenticated read to refuse. The walk is NON-WRITING.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing. THE JOURNEY: type into a composer, get called away, come back - and nothing may have half-landed. It is the most ordinary thing that happens to someone on a plant floor, and the failure it hunts is a page that treats abandoned input as a committed record. ★THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES THE VERDICT FAIR, and without which this oracle would punish good behaviour: after the reload the marker text is looked for in TWO places, and they mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD means a DRAFT was deliberately preserved - that is good UX and passes. Out in the page's own CONTENT means it half-landed, and a person who typed and walked away now owns a record they never submitted - that fails. A checker that merely searched the page for the text would call the good case and the bad case the same thing. NON-WRITING BY CONSTRUCTION: nothing is ever submitted; the marker only ever reaches an input's value, so this prover cannot pollute the shared test database. The composer inventory comes from tools/dialog_targets.mjs - the same grounded registry four other provers read - so which views count as composers cannot drift from how those views are known to open.FOR THIS PAGE AND PERSONA THERE IS NOTHING TO ABANDON. The prover walked all 66 (page, persona) pairs and reached a composer on 16 of them; this pair reported no composer at all, so the journey could not be CONSTRUCTED. ★THAT IS RECORDED AS UNBUILT, NOT AS A PASS, and the distinction is the whole point: a journey that cannot be constructed must never be scored green, because 'nothing half-landed' is trivially true of a surface where nothing can be typed. The prover carries that rail explicitly - non-vacuity, a journey that cannot be built is a finding rather than a quiet skip - and banking it green would be the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch. WHY THIS PAIR HAS NONE: the composer inventory is tools/dialog_targets.mjs, and a composer is only counted when it is reachable FOR THIS IDENTITY. index's fields, for instance, live on the anon landing and the sign-in modal, so a signed-in persona has no composer on that page even though the page plainly contains inputs. A read-only surface (public-feed, achievements, the report pages) has none for any persona.
